name: Ironpass Thermal Work Layer
description:
A heavyweight crew-neck thermal built for people who work outdoors in the Great Lakes corridor from October through April. The Ironpass is not stylish — it is effective. Double-knit construction with a waffle interior and a smooth exterior face, available in charcoal, navy, and a faded brick red. The collar is high enough to protect the neck from wind without being a turtleneck. Seams are flatlock-stitched to prevent bunching under gear. Thumb loops at the cuffs.

Construction crews, port workers, and utility teams all wear these. The fabric is dense and slightly stiff when new, softening over months of use into something almost comfortable. It smells faintly of the factory when new — a smell longtime wearers associate with the start of a cold season and a paycheck.
what_it_says: You work outside. You don't have time for anything that doesn't function. You've probably owned three of these.
story_hooks: A particular batch of Ironpass thermals was sold to a construction crew that vanished during a tunnel excavation project — some of the shirts have since shown up at Shelf market stalls.
Ironpass recently lost a contract with a major corponation and is quietly going under; workers who've worn nothing else for twenty years are facing a brand extinction.
A union organizer uses an Ironpass thermal as a kind of unofficial identifier — if you're wearing one at a certain meeting, you know what the meeting is really about.
